newsitem.title: USA: Cattle uptrend seen in jeopardy after USDA report.
newsitem.headline: Cattle uptrend seen in jeopardy after USDA report.

text.p: The recent strong uptrend in cattle prices appears to be in jeopardy following a bearish monthly cattle-on-feed report issued Friday by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, livestock analysts said.
The report showed that cattle marketings in June were lower than expected.

"We're starting to see some numbers which provide a backdrop for caution as we look at a slowdown in the marketing rate," Tom Tippens, chief executive of Professional Cattle Consultants, said at a CME market roundtable.
USDA put marketings in large lots in the leading seven states at 102 percent of a year ago, below analysts' average estimate of 104 percent.
Analysts said the report raised concerns that large premiums for deferred delivery and high replacement costs were prompting feedlots to keep cattle on feed longer and sell them at heavier weights.

"I think at this point we are seeing some things which are developing as a result of the premium markets and the overly optimistic attitude of the cattle feeders that I think throw up some red flags," Tippens said.
Tom Morgan, president of Morgan Research Group noted that seasonally adjusted steer weights in the Texas Panhandle were now the highest since the second quarter of 1996.
"Replacement costs are high, feed is cheap and we have too much premium in the back, and every time I've seen that in the past a disaster has happened," Morgan said.
Morgan said he was lowering his forecast for cash cattle prices as a result of the report and was now expecting prices to be in the low $60s for a while.
Cash cattle trade this week has been active at $64 and some had expected even higher prices next week, analysts said.
"Marketings in June have not kept pace with what we need to maintain at least a status quo. We have lost some currentness," Morgan said.
Dennis Kissler, president of KIS Futures, noted that contract highs had been set on both live and feeder cattle futures this week.
"I think you are going to see the futures market turn around on this kind of data and at least test last week's lows in the August feeders which is around 79.20 cents," he said.
August feeders on Friday rose to a peak of 83.05 cents, the highest level for the nearby month since February 1994.
Analysts said corn prices would be a key factor in determining the outlook for feeder cattle prices.
The key new crop December CBOT corn futures price rose to a peak of $2.58-1/2 this week, a gain of more than 30 cents since sinking to a contract low of $2.27-1/2 on July 7.
"If the corn market runs back to the $2.90 to $3.00 level it will probably put feeder cattle, at least in futures, back into the mid 70 (cent) range," he said.
